title: Kiran Chaudhary vs Amardeep Kaur on 29 June, 2026
full_text: Kiran Chaudhary vs Amardeep Kaur on 29 June, 2026 DLWT020132602021 IN THE COURT OF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS-06, DISTRICT- WEST, TIS HAZARI COURTS, DELHI PRESIDED BY: SH. GAURAV SINGAL, D.J.S. Kiran Chaudhary vs. Amardeep Kaur CC NI Act No. 2441-2021 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CNR number DLWT020132602021 2. Name of the complainant Kiran Chaudhary 3. Name of the accused and Amardeep Kaur W/o Sh. Bhupender residential address Singh, R/o D-50, Saraswati Garden, Delhi 4. Offence complained of or U/S 138 of Negotiable Instruments proved Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Conviction 7. Date of judgment/order 29.06.2026 Date of Institution: 12.11.2021 Date of Reserving Order: 03.06.2026 Date of Judgment: 29.06.2026 CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 1 of 22 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this Judgment, this court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by Smt. Kiran Chaudhary (hereinafter referred to as 'the complainant') against Smt. Amardeep Kaur (hereinafter referred to as 'the accused') under section 138 read with section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as 'the act'). BRIEF FACTS: 2. It is the case of the complainant that the accused was known to the complainant and had friendly relations. That the accused person asked for a friendly loan of Rs. 6,50,000 from the complainant on 30.04.2019 for starting up her business. 3. That the loan amount had been given to the accused partly in cash. That the accused also gave a written undertaking to repay the loan amount. That the accused defaulted in making the payment of the above-mentioned loan to the complainant and, in lieu of discharging her liability, the accused, in order to discharge the legally enforceable debt, issued the two postdated cheques in question. CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 2 of 22 DETAILS OF THE CHEQUES IN QUESTION: Serial Cheque Cheque Date of the Cheque Date of Reasons for No. number amount cheque drawn on return dishonour memo 1. 124562 Rs. 3,00,000 30.03.2021 Punjab 31.03.2021 Funds National Insufficient Bank 2. 414323 Rs. 1,00,000 30.03.2021 Yes 31.03.2021 Account Bank dormant 3.1 That the complainant presented the cheques at serials 1 and 2 to its banker at the State Bank of India, Mansarovar Garden, New Delhi. They were returned back vide memo dated 31.03.2021. The complainant, after receipt of the said dishonoured cheques, sent a legal notice dated 09.04.2021 in writing to the accused through its counsel, which returned undelivered at the address of the accused with the remark that "despite repeated visits, the premise was found locked on 12.04.2021, 13.04.2021, and 15.04.2021." It is, further, averred that the accused was duly served through WhatsApp by the complainant; however, the accused had failed to pay the cheque amount to the complainant within the stipulated time of 15 days. Hence, this complaint under the act was filed within the limitation period. CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 3 of 22 PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE COURT: 4. The file was received by way of transfer in this court on 09.01.2026. 5. After perusing the complaint and hearing the arguments of the complainant on the point of summoning of the accused, prima facie it appeared that the offence under section 138 of the act had been made out. Hence, cognizance of the offence was taken against the accused on 12.11.2021, and summon was issued to the accused. 6. Notice under section 251 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as " Cr.P.C .") was framed against the accused on 12.02.2025, to which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 6.1 At this stage, the accused admitted her signature on cheques in question but denied having filled the particulars therein. The accused stated that she didn't receive the legal demand notice; however, the accused admitted to her address as mentioned on the legal notice by further stating that the name of her husband is incorrect. 7. Thereafter, considering the defence stated at the time of framing of the notice by the accused, the court decided to allow cross-examination of the complainant as per 145(2) of the act, and the case was tried as a summons case. During the complainant's evidence, the complainant examined herself as sole witness CW-1. 7.1 The right of the accused to cross-examine the complainant was closed vide the order dated 09.05.2025, and the complainant's evidence was closed on CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 4 of 22 the same day. The statement of the accused under section 313 of the Cr.P.C. was recorded on 12.07.2025, wherein the accused stated that she will lead defence evidence. 7.2 However, despite multiple opportunities, the accused failed to lead defence evidence. Thus, defence evidence was closed on 25.09.2025. 7.3 On 03.06.2026, the final arguments of the parties were heard at length. EVIDENCE: 8. To prove the case, the complainant has examined herself as CW1 and has led her evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW1/A and has relied upon the following documents: Serial No. Document(s) Exhibit 1. Original Cheques CW1/1 (colly.) 2. Certified copy of the bank return memo CW1/2 (colly.) 3. The copy of legal demand notice dated 09.04.2021 CW1/3 4. The copy of the receipt of speed post CW1/4 5. The original returned legal notice envelop CW1/5 6. The copy of the handwritten acknowledgment CW1/6 (colly) 7. The copy of Whatsapp chats CW1/7 (colly) CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 5 of 22 9 The accused person has not examined any witness, and consequently, no document has been put on record by the accused person. 10. The Ld. Counsel for the complainant and the Ld. Counsel for the accused orally argued at length. I have carefully perused the record, including the written submission filed on record. ARGUMENTS: 11. ARGUMENTS ON BEHALF OF THE COMPLAINANT: A) The complainant, while reiterating the contents of the complaint, has argued that all the requirements of Section 138 of the act have been fulfilled by the complainant in the present case. B) That the accused has accepted the taking of a loan from him, which means that the accused has admitted to the existence of a legally enforceable debt. That the accused has also admitted to her signatures on the cheque. C) The complainant has further pointed out the contradiction of the accused, i.e., in the notice under section 251 of the Cr.P.C. and in the statement of the accused under section 313 of the Cr.P.C. The accused in the notice under section 251 of Cr.P.C. has stated that "I had borrowed a sum of Rs. 50,000/- and a sum of Rs. 70,000/- from the complainant at an interest of 10% before CORONA to further advance the same to one Poonam Sethi." The cheques in question were handed over by me as security. However in the statement of the accused under section 313 of the Cr.P.C., the accused has stated, "The CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 6 of 22 complainant had given loan of Rs. 1,00,000/- to Poonam Sethi and Anita." The complainant wanted to arrange funds from Sunita and asked me to give a blank cheque for the purpose of taking money from Sunita. The cheque was miused by the complainant." D) The complainant has further argued that the accused has not been able to raise any probable defence. Therefore, the accused shall be convicted for the offence under section 138 of the act with maximum punishment. 11. ARGUMENTS ON BEHALF OF THE ACCUSED: A) Per contra, the Ld. Counsel for the accused, while opposing the present case, has argued that the complainant has failed to establish legally enforceable debt against the accused. Thus, he argued that the complaint should be dismissed and the accused be acquitted. 13. Written submissions was filed by the complainant. Final arguments were heard for both the parties. 13.1 I have perused the record carefully. LEGAL PROVISIONS: 14. Before deciding the present complaint case, it would be pertinent to discuss the legal standards required to be met by both sides. In order to establish the offence under section 138 of the act, the complainant must fulfil all the essential CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 7 of 22 ingredients of the offence. The offence under section 138 of the act is made out against the drawer of the cheque only when all the ingredients highlighted below are fulfilled beyond reasonable doubt: I. Drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AMLBC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. 14.1 Section 139 of the act provides for a presumption in favour of a holder. It reads as under: "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in section 138 , for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability." 14.2 Section 146 of the act reads as under: "The court shall, in respect of every proceedings under this chapter on production of bank's slip or memo having thereon official mark denoting that CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 8 of 22 the cheque has dishonored, presume the fact of dishonor of such cheque, unless and until such fact is disproved." 14.3 Further, Section 118 Clause (a) of the act provides for presumptions regarding the consideration for the Negotiable Instruments. It reads as under: "That every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration". 14.4 The combined reading of the above-mentioned sections, raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. However, it is a settled principle of law that the presumption under section 139 of the act can be rebutted by the accused by raising a probable defence but the burden of proof is on the accused. 15. The principles pertaining to the presumptions and the onus of proof as recently summarized by the Honorable Apex Court in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418 as follows: "25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Section 118(a) and 139 , we now summarize the principles enumerated by this Court in the following manner: 25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of of the act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. 25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. 25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 9 of 22 preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. 25.4. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. 25.5. It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence." 16. Now, it is upon the accused to displace this presumption on a scale of preponderance of probabilities and the lack of consideration or a legally enforceable debt, but it need not be proved to the hilt or beyond all reasonable doubt. The accused can either prove that the liability did not exist or make the non-existence of liability so probable that a reasonable person ought, under the circumstances of the case, act on the supposition that it does not exist. Thus, the accused can do so either by leading his/her own evidence in defence or even by punching holes in the case of the complainant in cross-examination. 16.1 The accused has to come forth with a convincing defence that appeals to common sense and basic rationality. Only in a case where the accused comes up with a convincing defence to counter liability can the presumption be stated to have been rebutted. Because, once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. 16.2 In the case of Kishan Rao v. Shankar Gowda, (2018) 8 SCC 165, it was held that a mere denial of debt or liability cannot shift the onus of proof from accused to complainant. All that the accused needs to establish is a probable defence. CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 10 of 22 16.3 That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his/her defence. Section 139 of the act imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is also relevant to discuss the observation made in the case of Lekh Raj Sharma v. Yashpal Gupta (2015) 3 DLT (Cri) 521 by the Honorable High Court of Delhi as under: "The accused is obliged to set up a probable defence. The defence cannot be only a "possible" defence. It cannot be premised on the mere ipse dixit of the accused. There should be some credible material or circumstance available on record which should lead the Court to conclude that the defence/explanation for issuance of the dishonoured cheque is a probable one." 16.4 Further, in Kishan Rao v. Shankargouda , (2018) 8 SCC 165, quoting Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513, the Honorable Apex Court held as follows: "The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the non-existence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither permissible nor contemplated. At the same time it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of that, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumption the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on the complainant." CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 11 of 22 APPRECIATION OF EVIDENCE: 17. Coming to the present case, the accused has disputed the existence of the legal liability by stating that she had borrowed a sum of Rs. 50,000/- and a sum of Rs. 70,000/- from the complainant at an interest of 10% before CORONA to further advance the same to one Poonam Sethi. She acted as a guarantor in a loan transaction. The loan had already been paid back to the complainant by one named Poonam Sethi along with interest. The cheque was handed over by her as security, and the complainant has misused the cheque in question. She has evidence of the repayment of the loan. 18. The complainant has relied upon Ex. CW1/1 (colly.), Ex. CW1/2 (colly.), Ex. CW1/3, Ex. CW1/4, Ex. CW1/5, Ex. CW1/6 (colly.) and Ex. CW1/7 (colly.). The cross-examination of the complainant was closed vide the order dated 09.05.2025. 19. It is established by the CW1 that the cheques, Ex. CW1/1 (colly.), were presented within three months, and they were dishonored due to "Funds Insufficient" and "Account Dormant" vide memos bearing date 31.03.2021, which is Ex. CW1/2 (colly.). The ingredient qua the demand of the aforesaid cheques amount within 30 days of receipt of information of its dishonor has also been proved vide Ex. CW1/3, Ex. CW1/4, and CW1/5, which is the legal notice dated 09.04.2021 along with the postal receipt & the original returned envelope containing the legal demand notice, respectively. CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 12 of 22 19.1 The learned counsel for the accused submitted that the accused never received the legal demand notice. Hence, the present matter is liable to be dismissed. 19.2 The Honorable Supreme Court in K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan and another , AIR 1999 Supreme Court 3762, has observed that: If a strict interpretation is given that the drawer should have actually received the notice for the period of 15 days to start running no matter that the payee sent the notice on the correct address, a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by different strategies and he could escape-from the legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act. It must be borne in mind that Court should not adopt in interpretation which helps a dishonest evader and clips an honest payee as that would defeat the very legislative measure. Thus, when a notice is returned by the sendee as unclaimed such date would be the commencing date in reckoning the period of 15 days contemplated in clause (c) to the proviso of Section 138 of the Act. Of course such reckoning would be without prejudice to the right of the drawer of the cheque to show that he had no knowledge that the notice was brought to his address. In the present case the accused did not even attempt to discharge the burden to rebut the aforesaid presumption. 19.3 Even though the accused has denied receiving the legal demand notice, she has admitted that the address mentioned in the legal notice belongs to her. The legal notice was returned back undelivered with the remarks that "despite repeated visits, the premise was found locked on 12.04.2021, 13.04.2021, and 15.04.2021." The addressee as per the postal receipt, Ex. CW1/4, of the legal notice is Ms. Amardeep Kaur R/o D-50, Second Floor, Near Gurudwara Singh Sabha, Saraswati Garden, Ramesh Nagar, Delhi. Therefore, it can be presumed that the legal notice was delivered to the accused at her address. The accused has not brought anything on record to prove the contrary. A bald statement in the notice CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 13 of 22 under section 251 of the Cr.P.C. that the accused did not receive the legal notice is not sufficient. Moreover, the complainant submits that the legal notice was also sent via WhatsApp the accused. It is well settled that if notice is sent to the correct and last-known address of the accused via post, it is deemed to be served to him/her. In such a situation, the burden shifts onto the accused to prove that the legal demand notice was never served and that he was not responsible for such non-service. 19.4 Reliance is placed on Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which states that: 27. Meaning of service by post.--Where any 2[Central Act] or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression "serve" or either of the expressions "give" or "send" or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, pre-paying and posting by registered post, a letter containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post. 19.5 Reliance is placed upon the order dated 13.10.2023 in the case titled " Top Filling Point Proprietor Rakesh Agrawal v. State of U.P. and Another " and " C. C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr. " decided on 18.05.2007, wherein the Honorable Supreme Court held as follows: "In our opinion, therefore, when the notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing the drawer of the cheque, the mandatory requirement of issue of notice in terms of Clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the act stands complied with. It is needless to emphasise that the complaint must contain basic facts regarding the mode and manner of the issuance of notice to the drawer of the cheque." CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 14 of 22 19.6 The complainant has additionally depended on the copy of the written acknowledgment from the accused, i.e., Ex. CW1/6 (colly.) along with the screenshot of the WhatsApp conversation, i.e., Ex. CW1/7(colly). Nonetheless, regarding Ex. CW1/6 (colly.) is involved, neither was the original document presented to the court nor was the justification for producing the copy of the document adequately clarified. The primary document must be provided, or the requirements for the secondary document must be met. Additionally, Ex. CW1/7 (colly) lacks the necessary certificate required under section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Reliance is placed on Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal , AIR 2020 Supreme Court 490. 19.7 It is also not disputed that no payment was made within 15 days of the receipt/delivery of the legal demand notice. 20. The signature of the accused on Ex. CW1/1 (colly.) has not been denied. As per the scheme of the act, since the accused has admitted her signature on the cheque in question, it is presumed that the cheque in question, Ex. CW1/1 (colly.), was issued by the accused in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Thus, a presumption under Section 118 and Section 139 of the act was raised against the accused. 20.1 Referring to the act, a three-judge bench of the Honorable Supreme Court in T. Vasanthakumar Vs. Vijaykumari (2015) 8 SCC 378 has held the following: "9. Therefore, in the present case since the cheque as well as the signature has been accepted by the accused-respondent, the presumption under CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 15 of 22 Section 139 would operate. Thus the burden was on the accused to disprove the cheque or the existence of any legally recoverable debt or liability. 20.2 Once this presumption comes to the aid of the complainant, the onus is on the accused to establish his probable defence on a preponderance of probabilities; however, the accused need not necessarily step into the witness box to lead positive evidence, and he may discharge his onus of proof by pointing out deficiencies in the case of the complainant through effective cross-examination as discussed in earlier paragraphs. 21. Thus, the only ingredient that remains to be proved is whether the cheques were drawn by the accused for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. 21.1 The term "legally enforceable debt" is defined in the Explanation to Section 138 of the Indian Negotiable Instruments Act. It refers to a debt or other liability that can be lawfully recovered through the due process of law. In order for Section 138 of the act to apply, the debt or liability must be legally enforceable. As per Basalingappa (supra) to rebut the presumption and prove to the contrary, it is open to the accused to raise a probable defence, wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested. The words 'until the contrary is proved' occurring in Section 139 of the act do not mean that the accused must necessarily prove the negative that the instrument is not issued in discharge of any debt/liability, but the accused has two options. The first option is to prove that the debt/liability does not exist and conclusively establish with certainty that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt/liability. The CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 16 of 22 second option is to prove the non-existence of debt/liability by a preponderance of probabilities by referring to the circumstances of the case. 21.2 The accused, in the notice under section 251 of the Cr.P.C., admitted that the cheques in question were handed over to the complainant as security for the advancement of the loan and the entire amount had been repaid by Poonam Sethi. She has the proof of repayment. 21.3 In the statement recorded under section 313 of the Cr.P.C., the accused has stated that the complainant had given a loan of Rs. 1,00,000 to Poonam Sethi and Anita. She was a guarantor. The complainant asked her to arrange the funds from the two persons, to which she stated that they would not be paying right now. Then the complainant wanted to arrange funds from Sunita and asked her to give a blank cheque for the purpose of taking money from Sunita. The cheque was misused by the complainant. Further, she answered, "It is a matter of record" to question no. 2, i.e., that the cheques in question were dishonored for the reasons "funds insufficient" and "account dormant." 21.4 The right of the accused to cross-examine the complainant was closed via order dated 09.05.2025 after awarding sufficient opportunities. Also, the accused has not examined any witness, and the right of the accused to lead defence evidence was closed on 25.09.2025. 22. Aside from the declaration refuting legal responsibility, nothing was placed on record by the accused that shows or proves her defence raised at the time of framing of the notice under section 251 of the Cr.P.C. or at the time of recording CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 17 of 22 of her statement under section 313 of the Cr.P.C. However, the accused remained consistent on one aspect during the trial, which was that the cheques was given as 'security.' 22.1 The Honorable Supreme Court in the case of Sripati Singh (since deceased) through his son Gaurav Singh v. The State of Jharkhand & another (Cr. Appeal Nos. 1269-1270 of 2021) dated 28.10.2021 has held that the dishonor of cheque issued as a security can also attract offence under section 138 of the act. The Honorable Apex Court has observed as follows: "16. A cheque issued as security pursuant to a financial transaction cannot be considered as a worthless piece of paper under every circumstance. 'Security' in its true sense is the state of being safe and the security given for a loan is something given as a pledge of payment. It is given, deposited or pledged to make certain the fulfilment of an obligation to which the parties to the transaction are bound. If in a transaction, a loan is advanced and the borrower agrees to repay the amount in a specified timeframe and issues a cheque as security to secure such repayment; if the loan amount is not repaid in any other form before the due date or if there is no other understanding or agreement between the parties to defer the payment of amount, the cheque which is issued as security would mature for presentation and the drawee of the cheque would be entitled to present the same. On such presentation, if the same is dishonoured, the consequences contemplated under Section 138 and the other provisions of N.I. Act would flow. 22.2 The Honorable High Court of Delhi in the case of Suresh Chand Goyal v. Amit Singhal (2015) 3 BC 659 has also held as follows:- "28. There is no magic in the word "security cheque", such that, the moment the accused claims that the dishonoured cheque (in respect whereof a complaint under Section 138 of of the act is preferred) was given as a "security cheque", the Magistrate would acquit the accused. The expression "security cheque" is not a statutorily defined expression in the of the act. The of the act does not per se carve out an exception in respect of a 'security cheque' to say that a complaint in respect of such a cheque would not be maintainable. There can be mirade situations in which the cheque issued by the accused may be called as CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 18 of 22 security cheque, or may have been issued by way of a secu- rity, i.e. to provide an assurance or comfort to the drawee, that in case of failure of the primary consideration on the due date, or on the happening (or not happening) of a contingency, the security may be enforced. While in some situations, the dishonor of such a cheque may attract the penal provisions con- tained in Section 138 of the act, in others it may not." 22.3 In Jain P. Jose v. Santosh and anr., SLP (Crl.) No(s). 5241 of 2016, the Honorable Supreme Court has relied on the decision in Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar ," AIR 2019 Supreme Court 2446, where the court held that "even a blank cheque leaf, voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge of a debt. 22.4 The Honorable Supreme Court in the case of K. Ramesh v. K. Kothandaraman , 2024 SCC OnLine SC 531, in paragraph no. 5 of its order has observed as follows: "5. In this regard our attention was drawn to paragraphs 32, 33, 34 and 36 of the judgment in Bir Singh, wherein it has been observed that even if a blank cheque leaf is voluntarily signed and handed over by the accused towards some payment would attract the presumption under Section 139 of of the act and in absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued is discharge of the debt, the presumption would hold good. The said paragraphs are extracted below: "32. The proposition of law which emerges from the judgments referred to above is that the onus to rebut the presumption under Section 139 that the cheque has been issued in discharge of a debt or liability is on the accused and the fact that the cheque might be post-dated does not absolve the drawer of a cheque of the penal consequences of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. 33. A meaningful reading of the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act including, in particular, Sections 20 , 87 and 139 , makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 19 of 22 for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted. 34. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee, towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particulars. This in itself would not invalidate the cheque. The onus would still be on the accused to prove that the cheque was not in discharge of a debt or liability by adducing evidence." 22.5 Thus, in light of the above observations, this court finds legally recoverable debt exists in favour of the complainant to the tune of the amount mentioned in the cheques in question. 23. In view of the discussion above, it is apparent that the complainant has given a loan at a specific rate of interest, and for that amount cheques were handed over to the complainant. Therefore, the argument of the learned counsel for the accused that there is nothing on record to show that no loan was advanced fails, as the accused has herself admitted the same. 24. At the risk of repetition, the brief facts are that the complainant in her evidence affidavit, Ex. CW1/A, has categorically deposed that Ex. CW1/1 (colly) were issued by the accused in discharge of her liability qua the loan taken by her from the complainant. However, upon presentation by the complainant, the cheques in question were returned back with the remarks "funds insufficient" and "account dormant" vide return memo, Ex. CW1/2 (colly.) The complainant/CW1 has further deposed that the legal demand notice dated 09.04.2021, Ex. CW1/3, issued to the accused at her correct last-known address vide speed post Ex. CC No. 2441 of 2021 Kiran Chaudhary Versus Amardeep Kaur Page 20 of 22 CW1/4. The same was returned vide Ex. CW1/5, which is deemed served on the accused. Despite this, no payment has been made by her. 24.1 The testimony of CW1 has gone uncontroverted as the accused failed to cross-examine the complainant despite opportunities given. Further, the accused has also failed to lead evidence in her defence. As a result, nothing has come on record to establish the defence taken by the accused at the stage of framing of notice under section 251 of the Cr.P.C. or at the stage of recording of her statement under section 313 of the Cr.P.C. On the contrary, the accused has made contradictory statements qua the alleged payment made to the complainant. 25. Thus, in light of the aforesaid settled legal position & upon the appreciation of evidence on record, the court finds that the accused has not been able to establish any of the probable defence raised by the complainant and has failed to controvert the testimony of the complainant, and as such, the accused has not been able to rebut the presumption under section 118 read with section 139 of the act. Accordingly, the accused Amardeep Kaur is hereby convicted of the offence punishable under section 138 of the act. 26. A copy of this judgment be given free of cost to the convict.
